mainTopic: Valuing land when appraisers disagree, and selling half a field
overview: Three appraisers valued the same land at 80, 100, and 120 dinars. The first view in the ברייתא says it is worth 90. The גמרא challenges this with 'אדרבה': why not 110? It answers that the first two appraisers both keep the value at or below a hundred. אחרים divide the full range by three and get 93⅓, and the same challenge and the same answer follow. רב הונא rules like אחרים, and later like דייני גולה, who teach the same method. Each time, רב אשי objects that we don't understand the reasoning. A new משנה then teaches that when someone sells half a field, or the southern half, the halves are appraised. The buyer also gives up land for the fence and ditches. רבי יוחנן says the buyer takes the poorer half, and he proves from the southern-half case that the appraisal is about money. The גמרא then starts explaining how the two ditches are laid out, and this continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The first view explained: the land is worth ninety
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains the first view of the ברייתא. The land is really worth 90. The appraiser who said 80 was 10 too low, and the one who said 100 was 10 too high.
steps.simpleTranslation: The land is really worth ninety. The one who said twenty סלעים (80) was ten too low, and the one who said a מנה (100) was ten too high.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is explaining the thinking behind the first opinion: the true value is right between the low estimate and the middle estimate.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Twenty סלעים equals 80 dinars and a מנה equals 100 dinars. The first view assumes both appraisers missed by the same amount, so the true value is exactly in the middle, 90. The highest estimate (120) is set aside.

keyTerms.meaning: he made a mistake, he is off

phrases.english: is worth ninety;
and this one who says twenty
is mistaken by ten behind;
and this one who says a maneh
is mistaken by ten ahead.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the explanation of the ברייתא's first view, which began just before this point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The land is valued at 90: the 80-estimate and the 100-estimate each missed by 10.

steps.title: Challenge: maybe the land is worth one hundred and ten
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא flips the logic. Maybe the land is worth 110, so the 100-appraiser was 10 too low and the 120-appraiser was 10 too high.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! Say this land is worth one hundred and ten. The one who said a מנה was ten too low, and the one who said thirty סלעים (120) was ten too high!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the first view. The same 'split the difference' logic could just as easily be applied to the middle and high estimates instead.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first view averaged the low pair (80 and 100). Nothing obvious says we shouldn't average the high pair (100 and 120) instead, which gives 110. So why favor the lower pair?

keyTerms.meaning: on the contrary, the opposite could be said

phrases.english: On the contrary! This land
is worth one hundred and ten;
and this one who says a maneh
is mistaken by ten behind,
and this one who says thirty
is mistaken by ten ahead!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה! הַאי אַרְעָא מְאָה וְעַשְׂרָה שָׁוְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of step 1 by applying it to the other pair of estimates.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice to average the low and middle estimates (80 and 100).
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same logic works for the middle and high estimates, giving 110, so there is no clear reason to prefer 90.

steps.title: Answer: two appraisers keep the value at most a hundred
steps.stepSummary: Two of the three appraisers (80 and 100) agree the land is not worth more than 100. So the value cannot go up to 110.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, hold on to the first two in your hand: they do not take it out of the range of a hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It points out that the majority of appraisers keep the value at or below 100.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both the 80-appraiser and the 100-appraiser agree the land is worth no more than 100. Only one appraiser goes higher. So we stay within the range that two agree on, and 110 is ruled out.

keyTerms.meaning: at least hold on to, in any case grasp
from the category of, from the range of

steps.whatToRemember: The first view: average the low and middle estimates (90), because two appraisers agree the value is not above 100.

phrases.english: In any case, hold the first two in your hand,
phrases.notes: The first two are the appraisers who said 80 and 100.

phrases.english: for they do not take it out of the range of a maneh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 2.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Majority agreement sets an upper limit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The value might be 110, the average of the two higher estimates.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two appraisers agree the land is at most 100, so the value stays at or under 100 and 90 stands.

steps.title: The view of אחרים: divide the range by three
steps.stepSummary: אחרים say to take the gap between the lowest and highest estimates and divide it by three. That gives 93⅓, which is 13⅓ above 80 and 6⅔ below 100.
steps.simpleTranslation: אחרים say: you make an assessment of the gap between them and divide it by three. They hold the land is worth ninety-three and a third. The one who said twenty (80) was thirteen and a third too low, and the one who said a מנה was thirteen and a third too high.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the second opinion in the ברייתא, אחרים, and explains their math.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The gap from 80 to 120 is 40. One third of that is 13⅓, and adding it to 80 gives 93⅓. The גמרא pictures both the 80-appraiser and the 100-appraiser as missing by the same 13⅓, one too low and one too high.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Others', a תנא whose opinion is quoted under this name
an appraisal, an estimate of value

steps.confusionAlert: Don't get thrown by the math. If the true value is 93⅓, the 100-appraiser was really only 6⅔ too high, not 13⅓. The next step explains why the גמרא still says 13⅓.

phrases.english: Others say:
one makes an appraisal between them, and divides into three
phrases.notes: Take the gap between the lowest and highest estimates (80 to 120), split it into thirds, and add one third to the lowest.

phrases.english: they hold: this land
is worth ninety-three and a third;
this one who says twenty
is mistaken by thirteen and a third behind,
and this one who says a maneh
is mistaken by thirteen and a third ahead;

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲחֵרִים אוֹמְרִים: עוֹשִׂין שׁוּמָא בֵּינֵיהֶן, וּמְשַׁלְּשִׁין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the first view of the ברייתא to the view of אחרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The value is the lowest estimate plus one third of the range: 93⅓.

steps.title: Why the hundred-appraiser didn't say more
steps.stepSummary: By the logic of 13⅓, the 100-appraiser should really have said 106⅔. He held back because he felt going that far above his colleague was too much.
steps.simpleTranslation: By right he should have said more. The reason he didn't is that he thought: it's enough that I go this far above my colleague.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fills a gap in the explanation of אחרים. It explains why the 100-appraiser named a lower number than his 'mistake' would suggest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he truly overshot by 13⅓, his honest estimate would have been 93⅓ + 13⅓ = 106⅔. The גמרא says he rounded down to 100. He didn't want to stray too far above the 80-appraiser.

keyTerms.meaning: by right, it would have been proper

phrases.english: and by right he should have said more,
and the reason he didn't say it, he thought:
it is enough for me that I add
this much over my colleague.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains a detail in the math of step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The 100-appraiser rounded his estimate down so he would not go too far above his colleague.

steps.title: Challenge: maybe the land is worth one hundred thirteen and a third
steps.stepSummary: The same flip as before. Maybe the land is worth 113⅓. Then the 100-appraiser was 13⅓ too low, and the 120-appraiser was 13⅓ too high and held back.
steps.simpleTranslation: On the contrary! This land is worth one hundred thirteen and a third. The one who said a מנה was thirteen and a third too low, and the one who said thirty (120) was thirteen and a third too high. By right he should have said more, but he thought: it's enough that I go this far above my colleague!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges אחרים the same way it challenged the first view: why not measure the third down from the top instead of up from the bottom?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Counting one third down from 120 gives 113⅓. The same story about the high appraiser rounding down works just as well. So the math of אחרים seems to point either way.

keyTerms.meaning: I add more, I go higher

phrases.english: On the contrary, this land
is worth one hundred thirteen and a third;
this one who says a maneh
is mistaken by thirteen and a third behind,
and this one who says thirty
is mistaken by thirteen and a third ahead;
and by right he should have said more,
he thought: it is enough for me that I add
this much over my colleague!

steps.triggerLanguage: אַדְּרַבָּה, הָא אַרְעָא מְאָה וּתְלֵיסַר וּתְלָתָא שָׁוְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation of אחרים in steps 4 and 5, the same way step 2 attacked step 1.
steps.kashyaTarget: The choice of אחרים to add the third to the lowest estimate.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Subtracting the third from the highest estimate works equally well and gives 113⅓.

steps.title: Answer: again, two appraisers keep it at most a hundred
steps.stepSummary: Same answer as before: the first two appraisers agree the land is not above 100, so 113⅓ is ruled out.
steps.simpleTranslation: In any case, hold on to the first two in your hand: they do not take it out of the range of a hundred.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge to אחרים with the same answer it gave the first view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the 80-appraiser and the 100-appraiser both agree the value is no more than 100, we count up from the bottom. So 93⅓ stands. Both opinions share this principle and differ only in how they compute within that limit.
steps.whatToRemember: Both the first view (90) and אחרים (93⅓) refuse to go above 100, because two of the three appraisers agree the land is worth no more than that.

phrases.english: In any case, hold the first two in your hand,
for they do not take it out of the range of a hundred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 with the same reasoning as step 3.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Majority agreement sets an upper limit.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The value might be 113⅓, counting a third down from the top.
steps.terutzMaskana: Two appraisers cap the value at 100, so we count up from the bottom and the value is 93⅓.

steps.title: רב הונא rules like אחרים
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules that the הלכה follows אחרים, who divide the gap between the appraisals by three.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: the הלכה follows אחרים.
steps.whatsHappening: After all the back-and-forth about the three appraisers, רב הונא gives a practical ruling: we follow the method of אחרים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The method of אחרים was explained in Steps 4-7. You take the gap between the lowest and highest estimates, divide it by three, and add that to the lowest estimate. רב הונא now makes that method the practical הלכה.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Others': an unnamed תנא whose divide-by-three method was quoted earlier

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The halacha is like Acherim.
phrases.notes: אחרים are the ones from Step 4 who split the gap into thirds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a practical ruling after the method of אחרים was defended in Step 7.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows אחרים' divide-by-three method of appraisal.

steps.title: רב אשי objects to ruling like אחרים
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks how we can rule like אחרים when we do not understand their reasoning.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: We don't understand the reason of אחרים, and we should follow them as הלכה?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי pushes back on רב הונא's ruling. He finds it strange to rule like an opinion whose logic is unclear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier steps showed the method needed defending. Why exactly divide by three? Why should one appraiser 'hold back'? רב אשי's point is that a הלכה should rest on reasoning we understand, not just on a formula.

keyTerms.meaning: The reason or logic behind a view
We do not know or understand

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
We do not know the reason of Acherim,
and we should establish the halacha like them?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: טַעְמָא דַּאֲחֵרִים לָא יָדְעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב הונא's ruling in Step 8.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A הלכה should not be set by an opinion whose reasoning we cannot explain.

steps.title: The judges of the Diaspora teach the same method
steps.stepSummary: דייני גולה taught that an appraisal is made between the estimates and the gap is divided by three.
steps.simpleTranslation: The judges of the Diaspora taught: they make an appraisal between them, and divide by three.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching that gives the same divide-by-three method. It is from a different source, the judges of the Diaspora. This sets up a second ruling by רב הונא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same idea as אחרים, just in very short form. The appraisal is made between the extreme estimates, and the gap is split into thirds. The question will be whether this source fares any better.

phrases.english: The judges of the Diaspora taught:
They make an appraisal between them,
and divide it into thirds.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a second source with the same method as אחרים.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The gap between the appraisals is divided by three.

steps.title: רב הונא rules like the judges of the Diaspora
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא rules like דייני גולה.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: the הלכה follows the judges of the Diaspora.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא gives the same kind of ruling again, this time naming דייני גולה as the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since דייני גולה hold the same method as אחרים, this is really the same ruling. It is just tied to a different source.

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
The halacha is like the judges of the Diaspora.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב הוּנָא: הִלְכְתָא כְּדַיָּינֵי גוֹלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rules like the source just quoted.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows דייני גולה's divide-by-three method.

steps.title: רב אשי objects again
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי repeats his objection: we do not understand the reasoning of דייני גולה either.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: We don't understand the reason of the judges of the Diaspora, and we should follow them as הלכה?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי raises the same objection against this second ruling, word for word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Changing the source does not solve the problem. The method is the same, so the unclear logic is the same. The appraisal discussion ends here.
steps.whatToRemember: רב הונא rules like the divide-by-three method, whether it is quoted from אחרים or from דייני גולה. Each time, רב אשי objects that the reasoning behind it is not understood.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
We do not know the reason of the judges of the Diaspora,
and we should establish the halacha like them?!

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: טַעְמָא דְּדַיָּינֵי גוֹלָה לָא יָדְעִינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Repeats the Step 9 objection against Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב הונא's ruling like דייני גולה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Same as before: we should not rule like a view whose logic we cannot explain.

steps.title: משנה: selling half a field, or the southern half
steps.stepSummary: If someone sells half a field, or the southern half, the land is appraised and the buyer takes his half.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If one says to his friend, 'I am selling you half a field,' they appraise between them, and he takes half his field. If he says, 'I am selling you the southern half,' they appraise between them, and he takes the southern half.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts with two cases. In one the seller says 'half the field,' and in the other he says 'the southern half.' In both, the land is appraised and the buyer takes half.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The key word is משמנין, 'they appraise.' The משנה does not explain what the appraisal is for. That question becomes the center of the coming גמרא.

keyTerms.meaning: They appraise or estimate the value

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
One who says to his fellow:
'I am selling you half a field' –
they appraise between them,
phrases.notes: Between the two halves of the field. What the appraisal is for gets worked out in the גמרא.

phrases.english: and he takes half of his field.
'I am selling you its southern half' –
they appraise between them,
and he takes its southern half.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָאוֹמֵר לַחֲבֵירוֹ: חֲצִי שָׂדֶה אֲנִי מוֹכֵר לָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה and topic.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When half a field is sold, whether unspecified or the southern half, the halves are appraised and the buyer takes half.

steps.title: משנה: the buyer gives up room for the fence and ditches
steps.stepSummary: The buyer gives up the space for the dividing fence and ditches out of his half. A large ditch is six טפחים and a small one is three.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he accepts upon himself the place of the fence, the ditch, and the small ditch. How wide is a ditch? Six טפחים. And a small ditch is three.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה adds that the space for the dividing fence and ditches comes out of the buyer's half. It also gives the size of each ditch.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Splitting a field needs a fence and ditches between the two parts, and that takes up land. The משנה puts that loss on the buyer and fixes the widths: six טפחים for the large ditch and three for the small one.

phrases.english: And he accepts upon himself the place of the fence,
phrases.notes: 'He' is the buyer. The land for the fence comes out of his half.

phrases.english: the ditch and the small ditch.
And how wide is a ditch?
Six handbreadths.
And the small ditch – three.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה with a further rule about the division.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyer provides the land for the fence and ditches (6 and 3 טפחים).

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: the buyer takes the poorer half
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן says that when half a field is sold, the buyer takes the leaner, lower-quality part.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the buyer takes the lean part of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens with רבי יוחנן's rule about the first case of the משנה: the buyer gets the poorer part of the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The seller only said 'half a field.' So he can give the weaker half, since the buyer cannot demand better than what was clearly promised. This seems to clash with the משנה's word משמנין, which sounds like an even split.

phrases.english: GEMARA:
Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said
that Rabbi Yochanan said:
The buyer takes the lean part of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: לוֹקֵחַ נוֹטֵל כָּחוּשׁ שֶׁבּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the first אמורא's rule on the משנה's first case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a sale of 'half a field,' the buyer receives the poorer half.

steps.title: Challenge: the משנה says they appraise
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא challenges רבי יוחנן from the משנה's word משמנין.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said to רבי יוחנן: But we learned 'they appraise between them'!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חייא בר אבא asks a question on his own teacher. If the buyer simply gets the poor half, why does the משנה say the field is appraised?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An appraisal sounds like it is meant to make the two halves equal in value. That seems to contradict giving the buyer the poorer half.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said to Rabbi Yochanan:
But we learned: 'They appraise between them'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 15 from the wording of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's rule that the buyer takes the poorer half
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה requires an appraisal, which suggests an equal split, not automatically the poor half.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: we explained it from the second case
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן jabs that while רבי חייא was in Babylonia, they had already explained this from the later part of the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: While you were eating dates in Babylonia, we explained it from the סיפא.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers with a sharp comment: they worked this out while you were away. This sets up the actual proof, which comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His answer is that the second case of the משנה shows what משמנין really means. The proof itself is laid out next.

keyTerms.meaning: The later part of the משנה

phrases.english: He said to him:
While you were eating dates in Babylonia –
phrases.notes: A friendly dig: while you were busy elsewhere, we already settled this.

phrases.english: we explained it from the latter clause,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins the answer to Step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the משנה's word using its later clause
steps.terutzHavaAmina: משמנין means the halves are appraised so the buyer gets equal land.
steps.terutzMaskana: The later clause shows what the appraisal is really for (explained next).

steps.title: Proof: in the southern-half case the appraisal must be for money
steps.stepSummary: In the second case the buyer was promised the southern half, so the appraisal cannot be for choosing land. It must be for settling money.
steps.simpleTranslation: As the סיפא teaches: 'I am selling you the southern half' – they appraise between them, and he takes the southern half. Why appraise? He already told him 'the southern half'! Rather, it is for money.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן quotes the second case and asks: if the buyer was promised the south, what is there to appraise? He answers that the appraisal must be about money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the southern-half case, which land the buyer gets is already settled. So the appraisal cannot be about choosing land. It must measure the value difference between the two halves, so that one side can pay the other.
steps.confusionAlert: The appraisal does not change which piece of land the buyer gets. It only decides how much money is paid to make up the difference in value.

phrases.english: For the latter clause teaches:
'I am selling you its southern half' –
they appraise between them
and he takes its southern half.
But why do they appraise between them?
He told him 'the southern half'!
Rather, it is for money;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Lays out the proof promised in Step 17.
steps.raayaObject: That משמנין refers to money, not to choosing land
steps.raayaSupportSource: The סיפא of the משנה (the southern-half case)

steps.title: So in the first case too, the appraisal is for money
steps.stepSummary: The appraisal in the first case is also for money. The buyer takes the poorer half, and the value is settled with money.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is for money.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן applies the proof back to the first case. There too, משמנין is about money, so his rule stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The buyer can receive the poorer half, as רבי יוחנן said. The appraisal works out the value gap so it can be settled in money. That removes the contradiction רבי חייא בר אבא raised.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן says the buyer of 'half a field' gets the poorer half. The משנה's 'they appraise' is not about which land he gets. It is about the money value, as the southern-half case proves.
steps.whyThisMatters: This teaches a general reading tool: sometimes the later case in a משנה shows what an unclear word in the earlier case means.

phrases.english: Here too, it is for money.
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the first case of the משנה, plain 'half a field.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the proof from the סיפא back to the first case.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: משמנין in the first case refers to money, so רבי יוחנן's rule that the buyer takes the poorer half stands.

steps.title: Quoting the next clause of the משנה about the fence space
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words that the buyer takes upon himself the space for the fence, so that it can discuss them next.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: the buyer accepts upon himself the space for the fence, and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is quoting a new line from the משנה to set up the next discussion. Nothing is explained yet; this line just opens the topic.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion was about which half of the field the buyer gets. Now the focus moves to a different detail. The land for the fence and the ditches comes out of the buyer's half, not the seller's.

keyTerms.meaning: He accepts upon himself (he takes on the cost)
The space needed for a fence
"Etc.": the rest of the quoted line is assumed

phrases.english: He accepts upon himself the space for the fence, etc.
phrases.notes: The "etc." stands for the rest of the משנה's line, which also mentions a ditch and a smaller ditch.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the finished discussion about which half the buyer receives to a new clause in the same משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The buyer of half a field gives up land from his own share for the fence and ditches between the two halves.

steps.title: A ברייתא explains how the two ditches are arranged
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that the larger ditch is on the outside, the smaller ditch is on the inside, and both are behind the fence.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in a ברייתא: the ditch goes on the outside, and the smaller ditch goes on the inside. Both of them are behind the fence.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to explain where the fence and the two ditches mentioned in the משנה are placed. The explanation continues past this section.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only listed a fence, a ditch, and a smaller ditch. The ברייתא adds the layout. The larger ditch is farther out, the smaller one is closer in, and both sit behind the fence.

keyTerms.meaning: A smaller ditch (literally, the "son" of a ditch)

steps.confusionAlert: בֶּן חָרִיץ does not mean a second ditch dug by a different person. It is simply the smaller of the two ditches.

phrases.english: It was taught: the ditch is on the outside,
and the smaller ditch is on the inside.
And both this one and that one are behind the fence,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the arrangement of the fence and ditches mentioned in the משנה clause quoted in step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The larger ditch is on the outside, the smaller ditch is on the inside, and both are behind the fence.
